cards.question: What is training-serving skew and how do you prevent it?
options: A difference in hardware between training and serving; prevent by using identical GPUs
Features computed differently at training and inference time; prevent with shared transformation code or a feature store
Model weights drifting after deployment; prevent with checksums
Latency differences between batch and online inference
cards.explanation: Skew occurs when the same logical feature is produced by two code paths, typically a SQL or Spark pipeline offline and application code online, so definitions diverge subtly: different null handling, timezone, rounding, or unit. The model then sees inputs unlike anything it trained on and degrades silently, since nothing errors. Prevention: compute features with one shared implementation used by both paths, or use a feature store providing offline and online consistency by construction; log serving-time features and compare distributions against training; and add assertions on ranges and null rates in both paths.
cards.modelAnswer: Training-serving skew is when a feature is computed one way during training and a subtly different way at inference. The classic cause is two code paths for the same logical feature, a SQL or Spark job offline and application code online, and they diverge on details like null handling, timezone, unit, or rounding. It's insidious because nothing throws an error: the model just receives inputs unlike its training distribution and quietly gets worse, and it's one of the most common reasons a model that looked great offline underperforms in production. Prevention is architectural rather than procedural. Ideally one shared implementation of each transformation used by both paths, which is what a feature store buys you along with point-in-time correct historical lookups. Failing that, log the exact feature vectors served in production and continuously compare their distributions against training, since that comparison catches skew regardless of cause, and add explicit range and null-rate assertions in both paths so violations fail loudly instead of silently.

cards.question: What should be versioned to make an ML system reproducible?
options: The model weights only
Code, data, configuration and hyperparameters, environment/dependencies, and the resulting model artifact, linked together
The training notebook and the final metrics
The Docker image, which captures everything relevant
cards.explanation: Reproducibility needs the whole input set, not just the output. Code version (git SHA), the exact dataset snapshot (a hash or immutable dataset version, since 'the users table' changes daily), the full config including hyperparameters and random seeds, the environment (pinned dependencies and base image, plus CUDA/driver versions for numerics), and the produced artifact with its evaluation results. Crucially these must be linked, so from a deployed model you can retrieve exactly what produced it, which is what lets you debug, audit, and roll back. Full bitwise determinism on GPU is often impractical, so the realistic goal is provenance plus statistical reproducibility.
cards.modelAnswer: You need everything that determined the output, linked to the output. Code by git SHA. Data as an immutable snapshot or content hash, which is the piece people miss, because pointing at the users table means the training set changes daily and results become unreproducible by definition. Configuration including every hyperparameter and the random seeds. The environment, with pinned dependency versions and the base image, plus CUDA and driver versions if numerics matter. And the resulting artifact together with its evaluation results. The linkage is the important part: given a model running in production, I should be able to retrieve exactly the code, data, and config that produced it in one step, because that's what makes debugging a regression, satisfying an audit, or rolling back tractable. I'd also be realistic that bitwise determinism on GPUs is often impractical given nondeterministic kernels and reduction ordering, so the achievable goal is complete provenance plus statistical reproducibility, and I'd document which one I'm claiming.

cards.question: When is batch inference preferable to real-time serving?
options: Whenever the model is large
When predictions can be precomputed on a schedule and don't depend on fresh request-time input, which is simpler, cheaper, and more throughput-efficient
Only for models that cannot be containerized
When the model requires a GPU
cards.explanation: Batch scoring writes predictions to a store that the application reads, so serving is a cheap key lookup. It's far simpler operationally (no latency SLO, no autoscaling, retries are trivial, failures are non-user-facing) and much more efficient since you can use large batches and spot instances. It fits recommendations, risk scores, churn, and lead scoring where inputs change slowly. It fails when the prediction depends on request-time context, when the input space is too large to enumerate, or when freshness matters in seconds. A common hybrid is precomputing embeddings or candidates in batch and doing only lightweight ranking online.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd choose batch whenever the prediction doesn't depend on request-time input and can be precomputed on a schedule, because it's substantially simpler and cheaper. You score offline, write results to a key-value store or table, and the application does a lookup, so there's no latency SLO on the model, no autoscaling, retries are free, and a failed job isn't user-facing. You also get to use big batches and cheap preemptible capacity, so the cost per prediction is a fraction of online serving. It fits churn scores, risk scores, lead scoring, and recommendation candidate generation, where the inputs change on a daily rather than per-second basis. It breaks down when the prediction genuinely depends on what just happened in the request, when the input space is too large to enumerate ahead of time, or when the business needs seconds-fresh results. The pattern I'd reach for most often is actually the hybrid: precompute the expensive part, embeddings or a candidate set, in batch, and keep only cheap ranking or feature assembly online, which gets most of the cost benefit while remaining responsive.

cards.question: What is a canary or shadow deployment, and how do they differ?
options: They are the same thing under different vendor names
Canary sends a small slice of live traffic to the new model and observes real outcomes; shadow sends a copy of traffic to the new model but discards its output
Canary is for models; shadow is for infrastructure only
Shadow deployment replaces the old model instantly with automatic rollback
cards.explanation: Shadow (or mirror) mode runs the new model on real production inputs without its predictions affecting anyone, so it's zero-risk and validates latency, error rates, and prediction distributions against the incumbent, but it can't measure user response because nobody sees the output. Canary exposes a small percentage of real traffic to the new model, so you do get real outcome signal, at the cost of exposing some users to a potentially worse experience, which is why it's paired with automated rollback on guardrail breaches. The usual sequence is shadow to validate mechanics, then canary at a small percentage with monitoring, then progressive rollout.
cards.modelAnswer: Shadow mode, sometimes called mirroring, sends a copy of real production traffic to the new model but throws the predictions away, so no user is affected. That makes it zero-risk and it's excellent for validating the things that don't need a user: does it handle the real input distribution without errors, what's its actual latency under production load, and how does its prediction distribution compare to the incumbent on identical inputs. What it can't tell you is whether users respond better, because nobody sees the output. Canary sends a small percentage of live traffic to the new model for real, so you get genuine outcome and behavioral signal, but you're exposing some users to a possibly worse experience, which is why it needs guardrail monitoring with automated rollback on error rate, latency, or business metric breaches. In practice I'd sequence them: shadow first to shake out the mechanical failures cheaply, then canary at one to five percent with tight alerting, then progressive rollout while watching, keeping the old version warm for fast rollback.

cards.question: Why does prompt caching matter for LLM applications?
options: It stores complete responses so repeated questions are free
It caches the computed attention state for a repeated prompt prefix, cutting cost and time-to-first-token on subsequent calls sharing that prefix
It caches embeddings to speed up retrieval
It compresses prompts to fit more into the context window
cards.explanation: Prefill cost scales with prompt length, so a long system prompt, tool definitions, or a large shared document is recomputed on every request. Prompt caching stores the key/value state for that prefix so later requests reuse it, typically reducing cost substantially for cached tokens and materially cutting time-to-first-token. To exploit it you must keep the reusable content at the very beginning of the prompt and byte-identical, placing anything variable afterward, since a single differing character invalidates the cache from that point. It's distinct from semantic caching, which returns a previously generated answer for a similar query.
cards.modelAnswer: Prefill cost and time-to-first-token scale with prompt length, and in most real applications a large fraction of every prompt is identical across requests: a long system prompt, tool or function definitions, few-shot examples, or a document the user is asking multiple questions about. Prompt caching stores the computed key-value state for that prefix so subsequent requests skip recomputing it, which cuts both cost on the cached portion and latency to first token, and for long-prefix workloads like document Q&A or agents with big tool schemas it's one of the largest single wins available. The engineering requirement is prompt layout discipline: the cacheable content must sit at the very start and be byte-identical, with anything variable, the user's question, timestamps, retrieved chunks, placed after it, because a single differing character invalidates everything downstream of it. That means things like injecting the current time at the top of a system prompt silently destroy your cache hit rate. I'd distinguish it from semantic caching, which is a different layer that returns a previously generated answer for a semantically similar query and skips the model entirely.

cards.question: Why does continuous batching improve LLM throughput over static batching?
options: It uses larger batches, which are always more efficient
It lets finished sequences leave and new requests join at each decoding step, instead of the whole batch waiting for the longest generation
It batches requests by similarity so the KV cache can be shared
It moves batching from the GPU to the CPU
cards.explanation: With static batching, a batch is assembled, run to completion, and only then replaced, so if one request generates 1000 tokens and others finish at 20, the GPU spends most of its time computing padding for finished sequences while new requests wait in a queue. Continuous (iteration-level) batching schedules per decoding step: completed sequences are evicted and queued requests are admitted immediately, keeping the batch full. Since decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and a fuller batch amortizes each weight load across more sequences, this can improve throughput by several times, and it's why vLLM and TGI use it, typically alongside PagedAttention to manage the varying KV cache allocations.
cards.modelAnswer: The problem with static batching is that generation lengths vary enormously, so a batch runs until its longest sequence finishes. If one request generates a thousand tokens while the rest finish at twenty, you're computing padding for finished slots for most of the batch's life while newly arrived requests sit in a queue, so both utilization and latency suffer. Continuous batching, also called iteration-level scheduling, makes the batch composition dynamic: at every decoding step, finished sequences are evicted and waiting requests are admitted, so the batch stays full. That matters specifically because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, meaning the cost is dominated by streaming the weights once per step regardless of batch size, so packing more sequences into each step is nearly free throughput, and the gains are often several times over static batching. The complication it creates is memory management, since sequences of different and growing lengths come and go, which is exactly what PagedAttention solves by allocating the KV cache in fixed blocks like OS virtual memory rather than contiguous per-sequence buffers, eliminating fragmentation and enabling prefix sharing. That pairing is the core of vLLM and TGI.

cards.question: How do you choose between self-hosting an open model and calling a hosted API?
options: Self-host always, since it's cheaper at any scale
Weigh cost at your actual volume, data residency and compliance needs, latency and control requirements against engineering burden, quality gaps, and utilization risk
Use APIs for prototypes and always self-host in production
Decide purely on model quality benchmarks
cards.explanation: APIs win on time-to-market, access to frontier quality, zero ops, and elastic scaling with no idle cost, so they're the right default and the right choice at low or spiky volume. Self-hosting becomes attractive at sustained high volume where you can keep GPUs busy, when data cannot leave your environment for regulatory reasons, when you need custom fine-tunes or unusual control over decoding and batching, or when you need predictable cost and no vendor dependency. The honest costs of self-hosting are engineering time, GPU supply and reserved-capacity commitments, the fact that idle GPUs still bill, quality gaps versus frontier models on hard tasks, and ownership of your own reliability, security, and upgrade path. The realistic answer for most teams is hybrid: APIs for hard low-volume reasoning, a self-hosted small model for high-volume narrow tasks.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd frame it as five questions rather than a preference. Volume and utilization: hosted APIs bill per token with no idle cost, while a GPU bills whether or not it's busy, so self-hosting only pencils out at sustained high utilization, and spiky traffic is where it goes wrong because you provision for peak and pay for the trough. Compliance and data residency: if data legally cannot leave a boundary, or an agreement forbids third-party processing, that can decide it outright regardless of cost. Quality: frontier hosted models still lead on hard reasoning, so I'd ask whether my task needs that or whether a small open model with good retrieval clears the bar, which for narrow tasks it very often does. Control: self-hosting is what lets me run custom fine-tunes, control decoding and batching, guarantee no upstream model deprecation changes behavior under me, and hit tight predictable latency. And engineering cost, which people underestimate, since I now own capacity planning, GPU supply, upgrades, security, and reliability, and that's a team, not a weekend. My default is to start on an API to find out whether the product works at all, then measure actual token volume and quality requirements, and self-host the high-volume narrow workloads once the economics are clear. Most mature systems end up hybrid: a small self-hosted or fine-tuned model handling the bulk of easy traffic, escalating the hard minority to a frontier API.

cards.question: What belongs in CI for a machine learning project beyond normal unit tests?
options: Only linting and type checks, since model behavior can't be tested automatically
Data validation, pipeline smoke tests on a small sample, model quality gates on a fixed eval set, and checks for skew and artifact integrity
Full retraining on the complete dataset for every commit
Manual review of notebook outputs before merge
cards.explanation: Useful ML CI stages: schema and data validation (types, ranges, null rates, expected cardinalities) so bad data fails loudly; a fast end-to-end pipeline run on a tiny sample to catch shape and wiring errors without waiting for full training; deterministic unit tests for feature transformations, which is where silent bugs live; evaluation of the produced model against a versioned held-out set with a minimum-quality gate and a no-regression check, including per-slice results so an aggregate win can't mask a subgroup break; and a check that training and serving code produce identical features for identical inputs. For LLM applications add prompt-level regression tests and a safety/refusal suite. Full retraining per commit is usually too slow, so it runs on a schedule or on data/model changes.
cards.modelAnswer: Normal software CI plus several ML-specific stages. Data validation first, since most production ML incidents are data incidents: schema, types, ranges, null rates, and category cardinalities checked against expectations so a broken upstream job fails the pipeline loudly instead of silently training a worse model. Deterministic unit tests on feature transformation code, because that's where silent correctness bugs live and they're perfectly testable. A fast end-to-end smoke run of the whole pipeline on a tiny sample, which catches shape mismatches and wiring errors in a minute rather than after a four-hour training job. Then model quality gates: evaluate the produced artifact against a versioned held-out set with both a minimum absolute bar and a no-regression check against the current production model, and I'd insist on per-slice results in that gate, because an aggregate improvement that breaks one important segment should block. A skew check that training and serving code paths produce identical features for identical inputs. And artifact integrity, so the model loads, has the expected signature, and passes a few known-input assertions. For LLM applications I'd add prompt-level regression tests and a safety and refusal suite, run on every prompt change, since prompts are code and they're currently the least tested part of most systems. Full retraining is usually too slow for per-commit, so I'd trigger that on data or model changes, or on a schedule.

cards.question: How do you decide when to retrain a model?
options: On a fixed weekly schedule regardless of conditions
Trigger on measured degradation, drift, or sufficient new data, with a scheduled fallback, and validate every candidate before promotion
Only when users report problems
Continuously, with each new example applied as an online update
cards.explanation: Three trigger styles, usually combined. Performance-based is ideal but needs labels, so it only works where feedback is reasonably fast. Drift-based uses label-free signals (input distribution shift, prediction distribution shift) as an early proxy. Volume or schedule-based retrains when enough new data has accumulated or after a fixed period, which is a safety net rather than a diagnosis. Whichever fires, retraining must not auto-promote: the candidate is evaluated against the incumbent on a fixed held-out set plus recent data, gated on per-slice results, then shadow or canary deployed. Note that retraining fixes staleness, not bugs, so if the problem is a broken feature pipeline or a label quality issue, retraining just relearns the problem, which is why diagnosing before retraining matters.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd combine three triggers. Performance-based is the one I actually want: retrain when measured quality on real labeled outcomes drops below a threshold. It's the most direct signal but it requires labels arriving fast enough to act on, so it's viable for click prediction and not for loan defaults. Drift-based as the early-warning proxy where labels are slow: sustained input distribution shift or prediction distribution shift, which is available immediately and tells me something changed even if I can't yet tell whether quality suffered. And schedule or volume-based as a floor, retrain monthly or once N new examples accumulate, which is a safety net rather than a diagnosis. Whatever fires, the important discipline is that retraining doesn't mean promoting: the candidate gets evaluated against the incumbent on a fixed held-out set plus a recent time-based slice, gated on per-slice performance so it can't silently break a segment, then shadow or canary before full rollout, with the old model retained for rollback. The failure mode I'd warn about is treating retraining as a general remedy. It fixes staleness. If the actual problem is a broken feature pipeline, a label quality regression, or a concept change your features can't express, retraining faithfully relearns the problem and you've spent a cycle confirming the bug. So I'd diagnose before retraining rather than making it the reflex.

cards.question: What does a feature store provide?
options: A database of pretrained model weights
Consistent feature definitions served both offline for training with point-in-time correctness and online at low latency, plus reuse and discovery across teams
Automatic feature engineering from raw data
A cache of model predictions
cards.explanation: Its core value is solving two hard problems. First, offline-online consistency: one definition of a feature serves both the training pipeline and the low-latency online path, eliminating a major source of training-serving skew. Second, point-in-time correctness: when building a training set you must join each label with the feature values as they were at that moment, not current values, or you leak future information; feature stores implement that time-travel join, which is fiddly and easy to get wrong by hand. Secondary benefits are reuse and discovery across teams and backfilling. The cost is real infrastructure and operational complexity, so it's usually only worth it with multiple models, teams, and shared features rather than for a single model.
cards.modelAnswer: Two problems justify it, and both are genuinely hard to solve by hand. First, offline-online consistency: a feature is defined once and served both to the training pipeline in batch and to the online inference path at low latency, which structurally eliminates the most common cause of training-serving skew, namely two implementations drifting apart. Second, and this is the one people underrate, point-in-time correctness. When assembling a training set you have to join each label with the feature values as of that label's timestamp, not their current values, otherwise you leak information from after the prediction moment and your offline metrics are inflated. That as-of join across many feature tables with different update cadences is fiddly, and getting it subtly wrong is a classic silent leakage bug, so having it implemented once and correctly is real value. Beyond that you get reuse and discovery, so teams stop rebuilding the same customer-lifetime-value feature five slightly different ways, plus backfill support. The honest counterweight is that it's substantial infrastructure with real operational cost, so for a single model with a handful of features it's over-engineering, and I'd reach for it when there are several models and teams sharing features, or when point-in-time correctness has already bitten us.

cards.question: What are the main cost levers for a high-volume LLM application?
options: Only choosing a cheaper model
Model right-sizing and routing, prompt and context reduction, prompt/semantic caching, batching, output length limits, and moving work off the model entirely
Reducing the number of users served
Switching cloud providers
cards.explanation: Levers, roughly by typical impact: route by difficulty so a small cheap model handles the easy majority and only hard cases escalate; shrink the prompt, since long system prompts, oversized few-shot blocks, and excessive retrieved context are paid on every request; enable prompt caching for stable prefixes and semantic caching for repeated questions; batch aggressively when self-hosting, since decode throughput scales with batch size; cap output tokens, as output is usually the most expensive part and verbose responses are often worse anyway; quantize or distill a fine-tuned small model for narrow high-volume tasks; and remove the model from paths where deterministic code, a database query, or a classifier suffices. Measure cost per resolved task rather than per token so retries and human rework are counted, and attribute cost per feature and tenant so you know where money actually goes.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd order them by typical impact. First, routing and right-sizing: most traffic in a real application is easy, so classify difficulty and send the bulk to a small cheap model, escalating only the hard minority, which often cuts cost by a large multiple with little quality loss. Second, prompt and context reduction, because you pay for input tokens on every single call, so a bloated system prompt, oversized few-shot block, or twenty retrieved chunks where five would do is a permanent tax, and trimming context often improves quality too by reducing distraction. Third, caching at two levels: prompt caching for stable prefixes, which requires putting the invariant content first and keeping it byte-identical, and semantic caching to serve near-duplicate questions without calling the model at all, which in support workloads can absorb a large share of traffic. Fourth, output length, since output tokens usually cost several times input and verbose answers are often worse, so capping length and instructing concision saves money and improves the product simultaneously. Fifth, if self-hosting, batching and quantization, since decode throughput scales with batch size and quantization directly cuts the bytes moved per token. And sixth, the architectural one: take the model out of paths that don't need it, where a database query, a regex, or a small classifier is cheaper, faster, and more reliable. On measurement, I'd track cost per resolved task rather than per token, so retries and human rework are counted, and attribute spend per feature and per tenant, because you can't optimize what you can't localize, and unattributed LLM spend is how budgets get away from teams.

cards.question: How should an LLM application handle provider failures and rate limits?
options: Retry immediately until the request succeeds
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter on retryable errors only, with timeouts, circuit breakers, fallback models, and graceful degradation
Queue all requests and process them serially
Increase the rate limit request and wait for approval
cards.explanation: Immediate retries amplify an outage and, on a 429, actively worsen it. The pattern: classify errors, retrying only transient ones (429, 5xx, timeouts) and never invalid-request errors; use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms; honor Retry-After when provided; set explicit request timeouts, since a hung request holds resources; add a circuit breaker so a sustained outage fails fast instead of queueing indefinitely; and have a fallback path, a secondary provider or model, a cached or cheaper response, or an honest degraded experience. Also budget retries per user request so latency stays bounded, make handlers idempotent, and remember that for streaming responses a failure mid-stream needs its own handling since partial output was already sent.
cards.modelAnswer: Immediate retries are the wrong reflex, because on a rate limit they make things worse and during an outage they turn one failure into a retry storm. The pattern I'd implement starts with error classification: retry only transient failures, 429s, 5xxs, and timeouts, and never retry invalid-request errors since those will fail identically forever. Then exponential backoff with jitter, the jitter specifically so many clients don't synchronize their retries into a thundering herd, and honor Retry-After when the provider sends it since that's authoritative. Explicit request timeouts, because a hung connection holds a worker and cascades into your own capacity problem. A circuit breaker so that during a sustained outage you fail fast rather than queueing work you'll never drain, and recover with a probe rather than reopening the floodgates. Then fallbacks, which is where product thinking enters: a secondary provider or a smaller model, a cached or semantically cached answer, or an honest degraded experience, and I'd argue that a clear it's-unavailable message beats a thirty-second spinner. Some details that matter: budget total retries per user-facing request so latency stays bounded rather than multiplying, make handlers idempotent so a retry after a timeout that actually succeeded doesn't double-charge or double-send, and handle mid-stream failures separately since partial output has already reached the user. And I'd monitor rate-limit headroom proactively rather than discovering the ceiling during a traffic spike.

cards.question: What is the difference between model registry, artifact store, and experiment tracking?
options: They are three names for the same MLflow feature
Experiment tracking records runs and metrics for comparison, the artifact store holds the binary files, and the registry manages named versioned models with lifecycle stages
The registry stores training data; the artifact store stores code
Experiment tracking is for research and registries are for research too
cards.explanation: Experiment tracking captures each training run's parameters, metrics, and code version so you can compare and reproduce attempts, which is a research and iteration concern. The artifact store is the underlying blob storage for weights, checkpoints, plots, and datasets, addressed by run. The model registry sits above both as the production interface: a named model with numbered versions, lifecycle stages like staging and production, approval and lineage metadata, and the ability for a serving system to resolve 'current production version' without hardcoding a path. Conflating them causes real problems, notably deploying by copying a file from someone's run, which loses lineage and makes rollback and audit impossible.
cards.modelAnswer: They sit at different layers and conflating them causes real operational pain. Experiment tracking is the iteration layer: every training run logs its hyperparameters, metrics, code version, and environment, so I can compare fifty attempts, understand what helped, and reproduce a specific one. That's primarily a research-velocity tool. The artifact store is just the storage layer underneath, blob storage holding weights, checkpoints, plots, and dataset snapshots, addressed per run. The model registry is the production interface on top: a named model with numbered versions, lifecycle stages like staging, production, and archived, approval metadata, and lineage back to the run that produced it. The value is that a serving system asks for the current production version of a named model rather than hardcoding a path to somebody's checkpoint, which is what makes promotion, rollback, and audit tractable. The anti-pattern I'd call out is deploying by copying a file out of a run directory: it works exactly once, and then you can't answer what's running, what produced it, or how to roll back, which is precisely the question you'll be asked during an incident.

cards.question: How would you design observability for an LLM agent in production?
options: Log the final response and the total latency per request
Trace every step with linked spans: prompts, tool calls and results, token counts, costs, retries, and decisions, with sampling, privacy controls, and quality signals
Store all raw model outputs in a search index
Rely on the LLM provider's dashboard
cards.explanation: Agents fail in the middle, so a single request log is nearly useless for debugging. You need distributed-tracing-style structured traces: one trace per user request with a span per LLM call, retrieval, and tool invocation, capturing the exact rendered prompt, the response, model and version, token counts, cost, latency, retries, errors, and the reasoning or decision that led to each action, all linked by trace ID so you can replay a session. Add derived metrics on top (steps per task, tool failure rate, loop detection, cost per task, groundedness on sampled traces) plus alerting on those. Practical constraints matter: prompts and outputs contain user data, so you need redaction, retention limits, and access control; volume is large, so sample non-error traces while keeping all failures; and you should be able to replay a captured trace against a new prompt or model version, which turns production incidents directly into regression tests.
cards.modelAnswer: Agents fail in the middle of a trajectory, so per-request logging tells you almost nothing. I'd model it as distributed tracing: one trace per user request, with a span for every LLM call, retrieval, and tool invocation, linked by trace ID so I can reconstruct an entire session in order. Each span captures the exact rendered prompt including everything the model actually saw, the raw response, model name and version, token counts in and out, cost, latency, retries, errors, and where applicable the decision or reasoning that produced the next action. The reason I insist on the fully rendered prompt is that most agent bugs become obvious the moment you read what the model was actually given, and reconstructing it from templates plus variables after the fact is unreliable. On top of the traces I'd derive metrics and alerts: steps per completed task, tool call failure rates by tool, loop and repetition detection, cost per task with per-tenant attribution, and sampled quality signals like groundedness and task success. Then the practical constraints. Prompts and outputs contain user data and often PII, so I need field-level redaction, retention limits, and access controls on the trace store, and that has to be designed in rather than retrofitted after legal asks. Volume is high and traces are large, so I'd sample successful traces while retaining all errors and all flagged-quality sessions. And the capability I'd most want is replay: being able to take a captured production trace and re-run it against a new prompt or model version, because that turns every incident into a permanent regression test instead of a one-off fix.

cards.question: How do you meet a strict latency SLO for an LLM-backed feature?
options: Choose the fastest available model and accept the quality it gives
Budget the SLO across pipeline stages, then apply streaming, caching, parallelism, speculative decoding, right-sized models, and timeouts with degraded fallbacks
Increase GPU count until latency falls below the target
Move all inference to batch processing
cards.explanation: Start by defining what latency means to the user: for streaming interfaces, time-to-first-token usually matters far more than total completion time, and measuring p95/p99 rather than the mean is essential since tail latency drives complaints. Then decompose the budget across stages (auth, retrieval, rerank, prefill, decode, post-processing) and optimize where the time actually is. Levers: stream tokens so perceived latency drops immediately; cache prompts (cutting prefill) and semantically cache whole answers; parallelize independent stages instead of chaining them; cut input tokens, since prefill scales with prompt length; cap and shorten outputs, since decode is usually dominant; use a smaller or distilled model, possibly with better retrieval to preserve quality; apply speculative decoding for a lossless 2-3x on decode; and on the serving side use continuous batching while noting that batching trades per-request latency for throughput. Finally, enforce per-stage timeouts with a defined degraded path, so a slow optional stage like reranking is skipped rather than blowing the SLO.
cards.modelAnswer: First I'd define the SLO precisely, because latency for a streaming interface usually means time-to-first-token, not completion time, and those need completely different optimizations. And I'd hold it at p95 or p99, since the mean hides exactly the experiences that generate complaints. Then I'd decompose the budget across stages, auth, retrieval, reranking, prefill, decode, post-processing, and measure where the time actually goes rather than optimizing where I assume it is. From there the levers. Streaming first, because it's often the single largest perceived-latency win and changes the user's experience without changing the model. Caching next: prompt caching removes prefill for stable prefixes, and semantic caching can skip the model entirely for repeat questions. Parallelize anything independent, so lexical and vector retrieval run concurrently rather than sequentially, and start retrieval while validating input. Cut input tokens since prefill scales with prompt length, and cap output tokens since decode usually dominates total time and is directly proportional to length. Then model-level choices: a smaller or distilled model with stronger retrieval frequently beats a large model with weak context on both latency and quality, and speculative decoding gives a lossless two-to-three-times decode speedup if I control serving. On the serving side, continuous batching for throughput, while being explicit that batching trades per-request latency against throughput so I need to tune the batch policy against the SLO rather than maximizing utilization. Finally, enforcement: per-stage timeouts with a defined degraded path, so if reranking is slow I skip it and serve slightly worse results rather than breaching the SLO, and that degradation should be a designed product behavior with monitoring, not an accident.

cards.question: What security concerns are specific to deploying LLM applications?
options: Only standard web application security applies
Prompt injection and tool abuse, data exfiltration through outputs and context, training/RAG data poisoning, model output treated as trusted code, and denial of wallet
Only the risk of the model weights being stolen
Encryption in transit is sufficient since prompts are ephemeral
cards.explanation: Beyond normal web security, LLM-specific risks include: prompt injection, especially indirect injection from retrieved documents or tool output, which can hijack an agent's actions; excessive agency, where the model holds broader permissions than the user, so a successful injection escalates privileges; data exfiltration, since anything in context can be emitted, including other tenants' data if retrieval filters are wrong, and outbound channels like URL rendering or tool calls can leak it; insecure output handling, where generated SQL, shell commands, HTML, or code are executed or rendered without validation, creating classic injection and XSS through a new path; poisoning of RAG corpora or fine-tuning data, which is attractive because a single planted document can influence many answers; and denial of wallet, where expensive prompts or agent loops drive unbounded cost. Controls: least-privilege scoped tools, human approval for irreversible actions, egress allowlisting, treating all model output as untrusted input, enforcing ACLs in retrieval rather than in prompts, sandboxed execution, input/output classifiers, and per-tenant rate and spend limits.
cards.modelAnswer: Standard web security still applies, but there's a distinct class on top. Prompt injection is the headline, and the dangerous variant is indirect: instructions planted in a retrieved document, a webpage, an email, or a tool result that the agent reads and obeys. It's structurally hard because instructions and data share one channel with no privilege separation, so I treat it as a threat to mitigate rather than eliminate. That connects to excessive agency: if the agent's tools have broader permissions than the requesting user, a successful injection is a privilege escalation, so tools must be scoped to the user's own rights and irreversible or outward-facing actions need human approval. Data exfiltration is next: anything in context can be emitted, which means a retrieval filter bug becomes a cross-tenant data breach, and outbound channels are subtler than people expect, since rendering a model-supplied image URL or letting it make an HTTP call is enough to leak data, so egress allowlisting matters. Insecure output handling is the one teams most often miss: generated SQL, shell commands, HTML, or code executed or rendered without validation is classic injection and XSS arriving through a new door, so all model output is untrusted input to the next stage, executed in a sandbox with least privilege. Then poisoning of the RAG corpus or fine-tuning data, which is an attractive attack because one planted document can shape many answers, so I'd care about ingestion provenance. And denial of wallet, where crafted prompts or runaway agent loops generate unbounded spend, which needs per-tenant rate and cost caps and loop limits. Underneath all of it, the design principle I'd state is that the model is not a security boundary, so every control that matters is enforced in code outside it.

cards.question: Your LLM feature's cost per request tripled over two months with no code changes. How do you investigate?
options: Switch to a cheaper model immediately
Break cost into input tokens, output tokens, and call count per request, then find which grew: context creep, longer outputs, retry loops, cache misses, or traffic mix shift
Renegotiate pricing with the provider
Add a hard spend cap and move on
cards.explanation: Decompose before acting: cost per request equals calls per request times per-call tokens times price, so identify which factor moved. Common causes: context creep, where a growing knowledge base means retrieved chunks got longer or k crept up, or conversation history accumulates over longer sessions; output length growth from a prompt tweak or model version change; retry and agent loop increases from a flakier tool or upstream errors, which multiplies calls invisibly; prompt cache hit rate collapse because something variable was added near the top of the prompt, which is a very common and easily-missed regression; a silent provider-side model version change altering verbosity; and traffic mix shift, where a new customer or use case sends much larger inputs. The investigation needs per-request token and call attribution in your traces, segmented by feature, tenant, and route, and if you don't have it, adding it is the first fix. Then remediate the specific driver rather than downgrading the model reflexively.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd decompose before changing anything, because cost per request factors cleanly into calls per request times tokens per call times unit price, and each factor has different causes and fixes. So the first question is which one moved, and I'd want that segmented by feature, route, and tenant. If input tokens grew, the usual suspects are context creep: the knowledge base got bigger so retrieved chunks are longer or someone raised k, conversation history is accumulating over longer sessions without truncation, or a new document type parses into much larger chunks. If output tokens grew, either a prompt change relaxed length guidance or the provider silently updated the model version and it's more verbose, which is worth checking explicitly since it happens and it's invisible from my code. If call count grew, that's retries or agent loops, often caused by a flakier downstream tool, and it's the scariest one because a loop can multiply cost without any single request looking unusual. And if none of those changed per-request, then the mix shifted, meaning a new customer or use case with much larger payloads is now a big share of traffic, in which case per-tenant attribution finds it immediately. One cause I'd check early because it's common and easy to miss: prompt cache hit rate collapsing because something variable, a timestamp or a user ID, got added near the top of the prompt, which invalidates the cached prefix on every request and can triple cost with no visible code change nearby. Practically, if I can't answer these questions from my traces, then adding per-request token and call attribution is the first fix, since I'd otherwise be guessing. Then I'd remediate the actual driver rather than reflexively downgrading the model, which trades quality for a problem I haven't diagnosed.

cards.question: How do you handle a provider deprecating the model version your application depends on?
options: Pin the version indefinitely in the API call
Treat it as planned migration work: pin explicitly, maintain an eval suite to compare candidates, re-tune prompts for the new model, and roll out with canary and rollback
Switch to self-hosting to avoid the problem permanently
Wait until the deprecation date and swap the model string
cards.explanation: Model deprecation is inevitable with hosted APIs, so it should be an anticipated maintenance cycle rather than an emergency. Practices: always pin an explicit version rather than a floating alias, so behavior can't change under you unannounced, and monitor deprecation notices. Keep a versioned evaluation suite so a candidate model can be measured against the incumbent on your own distribution rather than on vendor benchmarks. Expect prompts to need re-tuning, since a prompt optimized over months for the old model is an artifact overfitted to it, and a fair comparison allows per-model prompt adaptation, so budget engineering time rather than treating it as a string swap. Watch for behavioral differences beyond quality, such as output format, verbosity, refusal boundaries, tool-calling reliability, and token counts that change cost and latency. Then roll out as a canary with guardrails and keep the ability to fall back until the old version is truly gone. Abstracting the provider behind an interface helps, but genuine portability comes from the eval suite, not the abstraction layer.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd treat it as a scheduled maintenance cycle rather than an incident, and most of the work is preparation that should already exist. Baseline hygiene: always call an explicit pinned version rather than a floating alias, so the model can't change under me without warning, and actually track deprecation announcements rather than discovering them from an error. When a migration comes, the critical asset is a versioned evaluation suite on my own traffic distribution, because vendor benchmarks won't tell me whether the new model is better at my task, and without that suite the migration is a guess. Then I'd expect real engineering work, not a string swap: a prompt tuned over months against the old model is overfitted to it, so a fair comparison means re-tuning prompts and few-shot examples for the new model, and I'd budget for that explicitly. I'd also look beyond quality scores at the things that break integrations: output format and verbosity changes that break downstream parsers, shifted refusal boundaries that cause new over-refusals on legitimate requests, tool-calling reliability differences, and token count changes that move both cost and latency. Rollout would be canary with guardrails and the old version kept live as a fallback until it's genuinely gone. On abstraction, I'd keep the provider behind an interface, but I'd be honest that a wrapper doesn't give real portability, since prompts, tool-calling formats, and behavior differ, so the eval suite is what actually makes me able to switch, not the abstraction layer. And I'd note that self-hosting trades this problem for owning upgrades, capacity, and security yourself rather than eliminating maintenance.

cards.question: What makes GPU capacity planning for LLM inference difficult?
options: GPU prices change frequently

Memory is dominated by weights plus a KV cache that grows with concurrency and context length, while throughput depends on batch composition, so capacity is a function of traffic shape rather than request count
GPUs cannot be autoscaled at all
Inference is CPU-bound in practice
cards.explanation: Unlike stateless web services, LLM capacity isn't linear in requests per second. Memory is weights plus activations plus the KV cache, and the cache scales with batch size times sequence length, so a few long-context sessions can consume as much memory as many short ones, meaning the same RPS can fit or OOM depending on prompt lengths. Throughput is also composition-dependent, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound, so a burst of long prompts starves token generation for everyone. Scaling is slow and coarse: GPU instances take minutes to start and load weights, capacity may be supply-constrained, and idle GPUs still cost full price, so you cannot scale reactively the way you would with stateless containers. Practical approach: capacity-plan in tokens per second and concurrent sequences rather than RPS, load-test with realistic prompt and output length distributions, cap max context and concurrency per tenant to bound worst-case memory, use continuous batching with PagedAttention to raise utilization, keep warm pools plus a queue with admission control, and consider a hosted API for burst overflow.
cards.modelAnswer: The core difficulty is that capacity isn't a function of request rate, it's a function of traffic shape. Memory is weights plus activations plus the KV cache, and the cache scales with concurrent sequences times their context length, so ten users with hundred-thousand-token contexts can consume more memory than a thousand users with short prompts. That means the same requests-per-second figure either fits comfortably or out-of-memories depending on prompt length distribution, and a single tenant pasting huge documents can destabilize a node. Throughput is composition-dependent too, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so a burst of long prompts consumes compute and stalls token generation for everyone already streaming, which shows up as inter-token latency spikes rather than errors. Then the scaling mechanics are unfavorable: GPU instances take minutes to boot and load tens of gigabytes of weights, so reactive autoscaling can't respond to a traffic spike the way stateless containers do, capacity may be genuinely supply-constrained rather than just expensive, and an idle GPU bills at full price, so over-provisioning has a hard cost. Practically I'd plan in tokens per second and concurrent sequences rather than RPS, load-test with realistic joint distributions of prompt and output length including the tail rather than an average, and bound the worst case explicitly with max context limits and per-tenant concurrency caps. Then raise utilization with continuous batching and PagedAttention, keep a warm pool sized to expected traffic with a queue and admission control so overload degrades into queueing rather than OOM crashes, and consider bursting overflow to a hosted API, which converts a capacity problem into a variable cost.

cards.question: How do you roll back a bad model deployment safely?
options: Redeploy the previous training run from the experiment tracker
Keep the previous version deployable and pre-validated, switch traffic back by config, then reconcile downstream state and data written under the bad version
Retrain from scratch with corrected data
Disable the feature until a fix is ready
cards.explanation: Fast rollback requires preparation, not heroics: the prior model version stays in the registry and ideally warm, traffic routing is a configuration change rather than a rebuild, and the rollback path is tested before you need it. The part teams get wrong is state, since rolling back the model does not undo its effects: predictions written to a store, actions the model triggered, records created or modified, caches populated with bad outputs, and any training data contaminated by the bad model's own outputs all need reconciliation, so you should know beforehand which of those exist and how to reverse or invalidate them. Also watch for coupled changes, because if the deployment included feature pipeline or schema changes, reverting only the model can create an incompatible combination, which is an argument for deploying model and feature changes together as one versioned unit. Afterwards, capture the failure as a permanent regression test so the same defect cannot ship twice, and review why pre-deployment gates missed it.
cards.modelAnswer: Rollback speed is decided before the incident, so the preparation is the answer. The previous version stays registered and ideally warm, traffic routing is a config or flag change rather than a rebuild and redeploy, and I've actually exercised the rollback path in a drill, because an untested rollback fails exactly when you need it. Then during the incident: switch traffic back first to stop the bleeding, and diagnose afterward rather than trying to understand the bug while users are affected. The part I'd emphasize because teams get it wrong is state reconciliation. Reverting the model does not undo what it did. Predictions may have been written to a serving store that downstream systems read, actions may have been triggered, records created or modified, caches populated with bad outputs that will keep serving them after rollback, and if the model's outputs feed future training data you've now contaminated your training set. So I'd want to know in advance which of those apply, and have a way to invalidate caches and identify and reverse or quarantine records written during the bad window. I'd also watch for coupled changes: if the release included feature pipeline or schema changes, reverting the model alone can produce a combination that was never tested, which argues for versioning model and feature logic together as one deployable unit. Afterwards, the real work is the postmortem: turn the failure into a permanent regression test so it can't ship twice, and ask specifically why the pre-deployment gates and canary monitoring didn't catch it, because that gap will otherwise let the next distinct failure through too.

cards.question: How do you serve many fine-tuned model variants cost-effectively?
options: Deploy each full fine-tune on its own dedicated GPU
Use LoRA adapters over one shared base model with multi-adapter serving, so many variants share weights and can be batched together
Merge all variants into a single model by weight averaging
Route all traffic to the largest variant and prompt it per customer
cards.explanation: Dedicated deployments per variant scale terribly: each holds a full copy of the weights in VRAM and each is separately underutilized, so cost grows linearly with variant count while utilization falls. LoRA changes the economics because adapters are megabytes rather than gigabytes, so one resident base model can serve many variants with adapters swapped or, better, applied per-sequence within a single batch, which is what S-LoRA and vLLM's multi-LoRA support do, letting requests for different customers share the same batch and weight load. Practical considerations: keep hot adapters in GPU memory and page cold ones from host memory or storage, accept a small throughput penalty from the un-merged adapter computation, and cap the number of concurrently active adapters. Alternatives when variants are few and similar: merge selected adapters into one model, or avoid per-customer models entirely by using one model with retrieval and prompt-level customization, which is usually the cheapest answer if quality permits.
cards.modelAnswer: Dedicated deployments per variant is the trap, because each one pins a full copy of the weights in VRAM and each is independently underutilized, so cost scales linearly with customer count while utilization goes down, which is the worst possible shape. LoRA fixes the economics: an adapter is megabytes against gigabytes of base weights, so one resident base model can back many variants. The naive version is swapping adapters per request, which works but serializes badly. The good version is multi-adapter batched serving, as in S-LoRA or vLLM's multi-LoRA support, where different requests in the same batch apply different adapters, so customers share one weight load and one batch, and that's what makes per-tenant models economically viable at all. Practically I'd keep hot adapters resident in GPU memory and page cold ones from host memory or object storage, accept a modest throughput penalty since un-merged adapter math is slower than a merged matmul, and cap concurrently active adapters to bound memory. I'd also mention the alternatives, because LoRA isn't always the right answer. If variants are few and similar, merging selected adapters into one model gives zero-overhead inference. And the question I'd ask first is whether per-customer models are needed at all, since one model plus retrieval of customer-specific context and prompt-level customization is dramatically cheaper to operate and often good enough, so I'd want evidence that fine-tuning per tenant actually buys measurable quality before committing to that operational complexity.

cards.question: What are the main data pipeline failure modes that silently degrade a production model?
options: Only outright pipeline crashes, which are always alerted
Silent schema changes, upstream default or null shifts, late or partial data, duplicate records, unit or encoding changes, and delayed label corruption
Slow queries that increase pipeline runtime
Insufficient storage capacity
cards.explanation: Crashes are easy because they page you. The dangerous failures succeed. Examples: an upstream team renames or repurposes a column, or changes a categorical encoding, so the feature still has valid values but different meaning; a sentinel default changes from null to 0 or -1, which the model reads as a real value; a partial load completes so aggregates are computed over incomplete data, making counts and rates quietly wrong; duplicate records inflate volume-based features; a unit changes from cents to dollars or a timezone shifts, so values are off by a constant factor; and label pipelines break so training data becomes systematically mislabeled, which is the worst case because retraining then actively makes the model worse. Defenses: schema contracts with upstream owners and alerting on schema change, distributional validation on every run (null rates, ranges, cardinality, row counts against expectation), freshness and completeness checks before training or serving, deduplication with explicit keys, comparing serving-time feature distributions to training, and validating labels themselves rather than assuming they're correct. Above all, treat data as a versioned, tested product rather than an input you happen to read.
cards.modelAnswer: The failures that page you are the easy ones. The dangerous class succeeds without error. Silent schema and semantic changes: an upstream team renames a column, repurposes it, or changes a categorical encoding, so my feature still contains plausible values with a different meaning, and nothing throws. Default and sentinel shifts, where a field that used to be null on missing now arrives as zero or negative one, and the model reads that as a real measurement rather than absence. Late or partial data, where a load completes with eighty percent of records so every aggregate, count, and rate is quietly wrong while the job reports success. Duplicates, which inflate volume-based features and can also leak across a train-test split. Unit and encoding changes, cents to dollars, a timezone shift, or a text encoding change that mangles categorical values into new levels. And the worst one, label pipeline corruption, because if labels become systematically wrong then retraining doesn't fix the model, it actively makes it worse while every metric computed against those same bad labels says it improved. Defenses: explicit schema contracts with upstream owners plus alerting on any schema change, distributional validation on every run covering null rates, ranges, cardinality, and row counts against expectation, freshness and completeness gates that block training or serving rather than warning, deduplication on explicit keys, and continuous comparison of serving-time feature distributions against training as a catch-all that detects skew whatever its cause. And I'd validate labels themselves rather than trusting them. The underlying stance is treating data as a versioned, tested product with owners and SLAs, not as an input I happen to read, because the majority of production ML incidents I've seen are data incidents wearing a model costume.

cards.question: How do you decide whether a task needs an LLM at all?
options: Use an LLM whenever the input is natural language
Ask whether the task needs open-ended language understanding or generation; if the input space is bounded or the rule is expressible, deterministic code or a small classifier is usually better
Use an LLM only if a small model scores below 90% accuracy
Always prototype with an LLM and keep it if it works
cards.explanation: LLMs are the right tool for open-ended understanding, generation, and tasks where enumerating the rules is impractical, and they're genuinely transformative there. But they're a poor fit where a deterministic alternative exists: parsing structured formats, applying explicit business rules, arithmetic and aggregation, exact lookup, and high-volume narrow classification where a fine-tuned small encoder is cheaper, faster, more consistent, and easier to test. The costs of an unnecessary LLM are nondeterminism that breaks testing and reproducibility, latency and per-request cost, an unbounded failure surface including hallucination and injection, and dependence on an external provider's roadmap. So the useful questions are: is the output space bounded, can a domain expert state the rule, does this need to be exactly right every time, and what's the volume? A common strong architecture uses the LLM narrowly, for intent extraction or converting language into structured parameters, and hands execution to deterministic code, which keeps flexibility at the edge and reliability in the core.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd ask whether the task genuinely requires open-ended language understanding or generation, because that's where LLMs are transformative, and reach for something simpler when it doesn't. The specific questions I find useful: is the output space bounded? Can a domain expert write down the rule? Does this need to be exactly right every single time? And what's the volume? If a task is parsing a structured format, applying explicit business rules, doing arithmetic or aggregation, or exact lookup, deterministic code is faster, cheaper, testable, and correct, and using a model there is strictly worse. For high-volume narrow classification, a fine-tuned small encoder is typically cheaper by orders of magnitude, lower latency, more consistent, and far easier to evaluate and monitor than prompting a large model. The costs of an unnecessary LLM are worth stating plainly: nondeterminism that makes testing and reproducibility hard, per-request cost and latency, an unbounded failure surface including hallucination and prompt injection that a regex simply doesn't have, and a dependency on an external provider's pricing and deprecation schedule. The architecture I'd advocate most often is hybrid and narrow: use the LLM for the part that genuinely needs language, typically extracting intent and converting a natural-language request into structured parameters, then hand execution to deterministic code that validates and performs the action. That keeps the flexibility where you need it and reliability where it matters, and it's much easier to test, since I can unit-test the deterministic core and evaluate only the extraction step. I'd also say the reverse case honestly: prototyping with an LLM to learn what the task even is, then replacing it with something cheaper once the requirements are clear, is a legitimate and often efficient path.

cards.question: What does responsible deployment require beyond model accuracy?
options: A privacy policy update and a terms-of-service disclaimer
Disaggregated performance analysis, human oversight for consequential decisions, transparency about capabilities and limits, contestability, and monitoring after launch
Compliance sign-off before launch, after which the model is the vendor's responsibility
Removing all demographic attributes from the training data
cards.explanation: Aggregate accuracy hides the failures that cause harm, so responsible deployment starts with disaggregated evaluation across groups and intersections, and with knowing which errors are severe rather than treating all errors as equal. For consequential decisions about people, keep a human genuinely in the loop, meaning they have the context, time, and authority to override, not just a rubber-stamp button, and provide affected people with an explanation and a real route to contest or appeal. Be transparent with users about what the system can and cannot do, since most misuse comes from mismatched expectations, and disclose when they're interacting with AI. Then treat launch as the beginning: monitor for drift and disparate impact, keep an incident and rollback path, and define who owns the outcome. Note the failure of two common shortcuts: dropping protected attributes doesn't remove bias, since proxies persist, and it destroys your ability to measure disparity; and treating this as a compliance checkbox handed to legal at the end tends to produce documentation rather than safer systems.
cards.modelAnswer: Accuracy is necessary and nowhere near sufficient, and I'd frame the additional requirements around who bears the cost when the system is wrong. First, disaggregated evaluation: an aggregate number routinely hides a subgroup where the model is unusable, so I'd measure across groups and intersections and treat a materially worse slice as blocking rather than as a footnote. I'd also distinguish error severity, because treating all errors as equal is how systems ship with rare catastrophic failure modes. Second, human oversight proportionate to stakes: for consequential decisions about people, a human in the loop who actually has the context, the time, and the authority to override, not a reviewer processing three hundred cases an hour clicking approve, which is oversight in name only. Third, contestability: an affected person should be able to learn that a model was involved, get an explanation they can act on, and have a real route to appeal, which in many jurisdictions is also becoming a legal requirement. Fourth, transparency about capabilities and limits, including disclosing that it's AI, because a large share of real-world harm comes from users trusting a system for something it was never validated to do. Fifth, treating launch as the start rather than the finish: monitoring for drift and for disparate impact over time, an incident and rollback path, and a named owner accountable for outcomes. And I'd flag two shortcuts that don't work. Dropping demographic attributes doesn't remove bias, since proxies like zip code carry it, and it removes my ability to detect disparity at all, so I'd keep those attributes for evaluation even where I exclude them from features. And handing this to legal at the end produces documentation rather than a safer system, so it has to shape design choices early, when changing them is still cheap.

cards.question: Design the deployment and operations plan for a customer-facing LLM support assistant. What do you prioritize?
options: Ship with the best model and a good prompt, then iterate based on user complaints
Establish evaluation, guardrails, escalation, and observability before launch, then roll out progressively with defined gates, cost controls, and a feedback loop into the eval set
Focus on maximizing containment rate to minimize support headcount
Build the full agentic tool integration first, since that delivers the most value
cards.explanation: A defensible plan, in order. Define success with the support org (resolution and containment rates, CSAT, escalation quality) and explicitly define unacceptable failures, which for support means confident wrong policy answers, promises the company can't honor, and mishandled vulnerable or angry customers. Build an eval set from real historical tickets covering common intents, the long tail, and those failure classes. Ground answers in retrieval over versioned help content with citations, since policy changes must propagate without retraining, and require abstention plus handoff when retrieval is weak. Design escalation as a first-class path with full context transfer, and make it easy for the user to reach a human, because trapping frustrated customers is the classic failure. Add guardrails: PII handling and redaction in logs, refusal boundaries, no commitments on refunds or legal matters without policy backing, and injection resistance since users control the input. Instrument traces, quality sampling, refusal and escalation rates, groundedness, and cost per conversation with per-tenant attribution. Roll out progressively: internal agents first with the assistant suggesting rather than sending, then a small traffic percentage on low-risk intents, expanding by intent as evidence accumulates, with rollback and kill switches. After launch, mine transcripts weekly, feed failures back into the eval set and the knowledge base, and watch containment against CSAT together, since optimizing containment alone degrades experience by suppressing escalation.
cards.modelAnswer: I'd sequence it so that the things that are expensive to retrofit come first. Before any launch, three foundations. Define success with the support organization rather than alone: resolution and containment rates, CSAT, escalation quality, and just as importantly a written list of unacceptable failures, which here means confidently stating wrong policy, promising a refund or commitment the company won't honor, and mishandling a vulnerable or distressed customer. Build the evaluation set from real historical tickets, covering high-frequency intents, the long tail, and specifically those failure classes. And ground the system in retrieval over versioned help-center and policy content with citations, because policy changes constantly and must propagate by reindexing rather than retraining, plus required abstention and handoff when retrieval is weak. Then the operational design. Escalation is a first-class feature, not a fallback: full conversation context transfers to the human agent, and reaching a human is always easy, because trapping a frustrated customer in a bot loop is the single most damaging failure and it's a product decision, not a model one. Guardrails: PII redaction in logs and traces, refusal boundaries around legal, medical, and financial commitments, and injection resistance since the user controls the input and will try things. Observability: per-conversation traces with rendered prompts, sampled quality and groundedness scoring, refusal and escalation rates, and cost per conversation. Rollout is progressive with gates: first internal, where the assistant drafts and a human agent sends, which harvests enormous labeled data at zero customer risk, then a small traffic share on low-risk intents like order status, then expand intent by intent as evidence accumulates, with a kill switch and rollback throughout. After launch the loop is what matters: mine transcripts weekly, feed every real failure into the eval set and every content gap into the knowledge base, and track containment against CSAT jointly, because optimizing containment in isolation just teaches the system to suppress escalation and quietly wrecks the customer experience while the dashboard improves. The one thing I'd push back on is leading with agentic actions like issuing refunds; I'd earn that with a proven read-only assistant first, because the blast radius of a tool-using agent on customer accounts is a different risk class entirely.
